fr:title.text: Benchmark cause of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Benchmark cause of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Build standalone Agda programs that measure typechecking time as a function of reindexing depth and proof style, to confirm or falsify the hypothesis that the slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties comes from nested reindexings combined with filler-at-a-time proofs (many transports over refl).

Constraint: do not edit the library. The benchmarks should be contrived client programs that import existing library code and exercise the suspected-pathological patterns at controlled depth, so the measurement is attributable to a specific shape rather than the library as a whole. Compare against the hcomp-en-masse alternative from the hcomp speedup note.

Output: a short writeup of which patterns are linear-vs-superlinear in depth and which are not, sufficient to decide whether Yoneda strictification actually attacks the right cost. This decision gates the broader strictification experiments outlined in the 2026-05-05 meeting notes.
Background: the original slowness observation and the hcomp-based workaround. Subtask of the Logical Relations on Display milestone.
Bench files live at Bench/ReindFillerChains/. The driver is run-bench.sh; REPS=3 ./run-bench.sh reduces variance.

html:ul.html:li: Flat (Implicit/Explicit{01..32}.agda): Postulated Z, X : Type, pt : Z → X, q : (z : Z) → Yᴰ (pt z), with mp = refl ∙∙ refl ∙∙ refl and a chain rectifyOut $ reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ ... ∙ reind-filler⁻ _ of length n. The Explicit variants fill {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻.

Wrapped (Wrapped{01,04}.agda): Mirrors the actual goal shape — outer rectifyOut/reind-filler⁻/congᴰ around a funExt₂/ΣPathP that splits Zᴰ-side from Xᴰ-side, with the inner chain on the Xᴰ-side. mp is still refl ∙∙ refl ∙∙ refl; types are still postulated.

Real (Real{00,01,02,03,04,08,16,32,64}.agda and variants Real04NoLossy, Real04AllRefl, Real04AllReflNoLossy, RealFlat04): Faithful re-derivation of ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ.universalⱽ.snd.fst from Sets/Properties.agda — imports the real SETᴰ, Fibers, AllLRⱽSETᴰ, isFibrationSETᴰ, and varies inner-chain depth, the --lossy-unification flag, and whether each reind-filler⁻ takes _ or refl as its path argument. Real00 has no proof body (baseline for the import cost). RealFlat04 has the depth-4 ∙-chain but none of the rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP wrapping — it controls for the wrapping vs. the chain alone.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each measured run deletes that file's .agdai so only the bench file is rechecked; library and Properties.agda imports are cached.
Wall time, single run on the dev machine. Library-import cost has been warmed out — these numbers reflect rechecking only the bench file.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: STYLE DEPTH TIME(s) Δ-base(s) Implicit 01 0.87 -0.01 Implicit 02 0.86 -0.02 Implicit 04 0.90 +0.02 Implicit 08 0.86 -0.02 Implicit 16 0.86 -0.02 Implicit 32 ~0.87 ~0 Explicit 01 0.88 0.00 Explicit 16 0.86 -0.02
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Flat reind-filler⁻ chains over postulated types are not slow at any depth, regardless of whether implicits are filled. Up through 32 nested reind-filler⁻'s the marginal cost is below measurement noise.
Adding the rectifyOut/reind-filler⁻/congᴰ + funExt₂/ΣPathP wrapping over postulated types is also not slow. The shape alone is not the problem.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
FILE TIME(s) Δ-base(s) Real00 (no proof) 3.37 0.00 -- imports only Real01 3.37 0.00 Real02 3.82 0.45 Real03 4.07 0.70 Real04 12.97 9.60 <-- jump Real08 13.19 9.82 Real16 13.40 10.03
Real04NoLossy 213.15 209.78 -- --lossy-unification removed
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Real family reproduces the slowness from Sets/Properties.agda. Three findings:

html:ol.html:li: Apparent step function at depth 4 is "first successful elaboration", not a unifier threshold: Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify (see Open Questions). Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, after which post-typing work fires. Past depth 4 the cost plateaus (~30ms per added junction through depth 64), so the chain length itself is not the expensive part.

Lossy-unification dominates: removing --lossy-unification turns the depth-4 case from ~13s into 213s — a 16× blowup. The flat ∙-chain over real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types is what lossy bounds; without it the unifier does real work on every junction trying to normalize the deeply-nested fiber types.

Postulated types don't trigger this: Wrapped04 (same shape, postulated types, refl-equivalent mp) is fast — the unifier blowup is type-driven. The cost is in unifying SETᴰ hom-types — concretely Hom[ Z , X ][ Zᴰ , g*Xᴰ ] where g*Xᴰ unfolds through isFibrationSETᴰ._*_, presheaf reindexing, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc. — not in unifying reind-filler⁻ implicits over a postulated P : (Z → X) → Type.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Where the time goes inside Agda, with --lossy-unification on. agda --profile=internal Real04.agda (cache warmed, only the bench file rechecked):
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
Real04 Real00-noBody RealFlat04 Total 14,969ms 3,105ms 1,389ms Typing 193ms 2ms 6ms Typing.OccursCheck 186ms - - Typing.CheckRHS 60ms - - Scoping.InverseNameLookup 3,756ms - - Miscellaneous 3,723ms 26ms 27ms Deserialization 3,084ms 2,928ms 1,275ms Highlighting 2,464ms - - Serialization.BuildInterface 1,299ms - - metas 384 73 174
Typing share of total in Real04: 193 / 14,969 = 1.3 percent.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Real00 has no proof body and only imports Properties.agda (3.1s, of which 2.9s is interface deserialization — fixed cost, cache-driven). RealFlat04 has the depth-4 ∙-chain on real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types but no wrapping — no rectifyOut, no congᴰ, no funExt₂, no ΣPathP. It costs 1.39s.
So adding the wrapped proof body on top of the import skeleton spends:

html:ul.html:li: ~450ms on actual typing/unification under lossy (the ∙-chain over SETᴰ.Hom types — what --lossy-unification bounds, and what the _ → refl annotation further cuts).
~11.5s on post-typing bookkeeping: scope-name lookup, the Miscellaneous bucket, syntax highlighting, building the interface — driven by the size of the unsolved meta store.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Without --lossy-unification, the typing budget rises from ~450ms to ~210s and dominates everything else; lossy is doing essential work even though it doesn't show up as a big slice of the profile under the lossy run. The annotation experiment subtree below quantifies what's left of the typing budget after lossy and how to attack it further.

fr:title.text: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing --allow-unsolved-metas from Real04 fails with [UnsolvedConstraints]. Same for RealFlat04. So with --lossy-unification on, Agda doesn't actually finish elaborating the proof. The body persisted to the interface is a single reference to an unsolved meta (unsolvedmeta.N) parameterised by the module's level args. The "elaborated term" I attributed the cost to in earlier drafts of this tree doesn't exist.

What does exist in the meta-store: 384 unsolved metas for Real04, 174 for RealFlat04, 73 for Real00. Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: GOAL ELABORATED AST NODES AGDA WALL TIME Implicit01 55 0.87s Implicit04 688 0.90s Implicit16 8,350 0.86s Implicit32 31,334 0.87s Wrapped01 688 0.97s Wrapped04 1,507 0.98s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.

The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.

The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.

fr:title.text: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.

The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:

html:ul.html:li: Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.

Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.

Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.

The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.

Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).

It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.

It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:

html:ul.html:li: --lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.

fr:title.text: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:mainmatter.html:p: User hypothesis: "many unification problems with dependencies, where later problems depend on earlier ones; filling sufficient annotations should disambiguate and give a big speedup." Tested by replacing each _ argument to reind-filler⁻ with refl.
Bench fixture: Bench/ReindFillerChains/Real04AllRefl.agda. Wall times under --lossy-unification --allow-unsolved-metas:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, lossy) 13.13 s 384 metas Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, lossy) 6.20 s 389 metas Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, NO lossy) 213 s -- Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, NO lossy) 203.82 s --
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Confirmed in the actual library by uncommenting ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/Instances/Sets/Properties.agda (.snd.snd left as a hole, matching the pre-existing comment) and toggling the same _ ↔ refl change:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Properties.agda (Exp commented out) 3.79 s Properties.agda (Exp live, `_` × 6) 14.83 s Properties.agda (Exp live, refl × 6) 6.75 s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: 2.18× speedup in the real file. The bench was faithful — the same change that worked on the contrived bench works on the actual definition. Caveat: the _s in isFibrationSETᴰueⱽ and BinProductsⱽSETᴰueⱽ do not accept refl (those fillers produce non-trivial paths, unlike the rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain inside Exp). The intervention is specific to wrapped reindexing chains.

html:ul.html:li: Lossy attacks per-meta type complexity. It bounds how much work the unifier does normalizing the huge SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types attached to each meta.

Annotation attacks per-meta unifier work. Even after lossy makes each meta tractable, the unifier still spends real time searching for e : a ≡ b at each reind-filler⁻ call. Handing it refl short-circuits that search.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Meta count is essentially unchanged (384 → 389, basically noise). The user's hypothesis that "filling earlier metas resolves later ones" is not what's happening — invisible metas like _b_237, _a_276, _bᴰ.fst_358 survive both runs. Annotation reduces work per meta, not number of metas.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.

This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. The investigation here just quantifies what that interactive workflow was achieving.

Caveat: writing refl only works because, in this specific proof shape, every e : a ≡ b arising from reind-filler⁻ reduces under the rectifyOut/congᴰ wrapping to a path of compositions that collapses to refl once the implicit fiber types are pinned. In a more general chain you might need a non-trivial composite — but in that case C-u C-u C-c C-s still gives the right thing.

Decision implication: strictification + lossy + explicit refl are the three independent levers. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest factor (per-meta type complexity, multiplicatively shrinks meta sizes); the _→refl cleanup is a cheap mechanical 2× before doing any structural work.

html:ul.html:li: The depth 3→4 step (Real03 = 4.07s, Real04 = 12.97s) is now understood as "first successful elaboration", not a lossy threshold. Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify. Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, at which point the post-typing bookkeeping fires. Worth confirming by a typecheck-only benchmark that disables Highlighting and Serialization, if Agda exposes the knobs.

Does the refl-annotation lever transfer to the UniversalQuantifierⱽ proof shape? ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ benefits 2× because its rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain reduces to refl once implicits are pinned. The non-Eq UQ counterpart isn't written in the library yet (the legacy commented block in Sets/Properties.agda uses an obsolete API). When someone is already inside that file, attempting the construction is the cheapest way to find out.

Does the snd .snd field (currently a {!!} hole in ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ and in the bench files) have the same shape when filled? It would add another rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP block and (per the cost model) multiply the meta count again.

Is Scoping.InverseNameLookup actually triggered by typing-time pretty-printing of constraints, in which case it's partly typing cost masquerading as bookkeeping? Highlighting and Serialization (3.76s combined) are unambiguously post-typing; the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup attribution is fuzzier. The qualitative claim ("typing under lossy is a small slice, meta-store bookkeeping dominates") holds either way.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Orchestration tree for finishing the paper Logical Relations on Display. Not a TODO itself; groups and tracks the subtasks below. Status lives on the individual subtask trees.

Goal. A submittable draft that (i) uses consistent, well-explained notation, (ii) situates the work against Twelf, Synthetic Tait Computability, and other mechanized-metatheory approaches, and (iii) demonstrates the framework on a fully worked presented-categories example with equational axioms.

Audit and fix the notation throughout Logical Relations on Display. Current notation is inconsistent and, in places, unexplained. Make a pass that (i) establishes a single convention per concept, (ii) introduces each piece of notation where it is first used, and (iii) updates figures and inline math accordingly.
Subtask of the Finishing Logical Relations on Display milestone.

Give the body of Logical Relations on Display a better narrative arc. The current draft presents the technical material but does not carry a reader through the argument. Identify the central story, rearrange sections to serve it, and add connective tissue between the setup, the general framework, and the worked example.
Subtask of the Finishing Logical Relations on Display milestone.

Write the related works section of Logical Relations on Display. The section needs to motivate the occasion for better mechanized metatheory by speaking to the drawbacks of existing approaches — in particular Twelf and Synthetic Tait Computability — and position the displayed-logical-relations approach against them.
This subtask absorbs the content of the cancelled Review related approaches to metatheory TODO.
Subtask of the Finishing Logical Relations on Display milestone.

Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: GOAL ELABORATED AST NODES AGDA WALL TIME Implicit01 55 0.87s Implicit04 688 0.90s Implicit16 8,350 0.86s Implicit32 31,334 0.87s Wrapped01 688 0.97s Wrapped04 1,507 0.98s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.

The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.

The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.

fr:title.text: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.

The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:

html:ul.html:li: Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.

Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.

Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.

The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.

Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).

It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.

It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:

html:ul.html:li: --lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.

fr:title.text: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:mainmatter.html:p: User hypothesis: "many unification problems with dependencies, where later problems depend on earlier ones; filling sufficient annotations should disambiguate and give a big speedup." Tested by replacing each _ argument to reind-filler⁻ with refl.
Bench fixture: Bench/ReindFillerChains/Real04AllRefl.agda. Wall times under --lossy-unification --allow-unsolved-metas:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, lossy) 13.13 s 384 metas Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, lossy) 6.20 s 389 metas Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, NO lossy) 213 s -- Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, NO lossy) 203.82 s --
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Confirmed in the actual library by uncommenting ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/Instances/Sets/Properties.agda (.snd.snd left as a hole, matching the pre-existing comment) and toggling the same _ ↔ refl change:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Properties.agda (Exp commented out) 3.79 s Properties.agda (Exp live, `_` × 6) 14.83 s Properties.agda (Exp live, refl × 6) 6.75 s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: 2.18× speedup in the real file. The bench was faithful — the same change that worked on the contrived bench works on the actual definition. Caveat: the _s in isFibrationSETᴰueⱽ and BinProductsⱽSETᴰueⱽ do not accept refl (those fillers produce non-trivial paths, unlike the rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain inside Exp). The intervention is specific to wrapped reindexing chains.

html:ul.html:li: Lossy attacks per-meta type complexity. It bounds how much work the unifier does normalizing the huge SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types attached to each meta.

Annotation attacks per-meta unifier work. Even after lossy makes each meta tractable, the unifier still spends real time searching for e : a ≡ b at each reind-filler⁻ call. Handing it refl short-circuits that search.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Meta count is essentially unchanged (384 → 389, basically noise). The user's hypothesis that "filling earlier metas resolves later ones" is not what's happening — invisible metas like _b_237, _a_276, _bᴰ.fst_358 survive both runs. Annotation reduces work per meta, not number of metas.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.

This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. The investigation here just quantifies what that interactive workflow was achieving.

Caveat: writing refl only works because, in this specific proof shape, every e : a ≡ b arising from reind-filler⁻ reduces under the rectifyOut/congᴰ wrapping to a path of compositions that collapses to refl once the implicit fiber types are pinned. In a more general chain you might need a non-trivial composite — but in that case C-u C-u C-c C-s still gives the right thing.

Decision implication: strictification + lossy + explicit refl are the three independent levers. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest factor (per-meta type complexity, multiplicatively shrinks meta sizes); the _→refl cleanup is a cheap mechanical 2× before doing any structural work.

html:ul.html:li: The depth 3→4 step (Real03 = 4.07s, Real04 = 12.97s) is now understood as "first successful elaboration", not a lossy threshold. Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify. Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, at which point the post-typing bookkeeping fires. Worth confirming by a typecheck-only benchmark that disables Highlighting and Serialization, if Agda exposes the knobs.

Does the refl-annotation lever transfer to the UniversalQuantifierⱽ proof shape? ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ benefits 2× because its rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain reduces to refl once implicits are pinned. The non-Eq UQ counterpart isn't written in the library yet (the legacy commented block in Sets/Properties.agda uses an obsolete API). When someone is already inside that file, attempting the construction is the cheapest way to find out.

Does the snd .snd field (currently a {!!} hole in ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ and in the bench files) have the same shape when filled? It would add another rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP block and (per the cost model) multiply the meta count again.

Is Scoping.InverseNameLookup actually triggered by typing-time pretty-printing of constraints, in which case it's partly typing cost masquerading as bookkeeping? Highlighting and Serialization (3.76s combined) are unambiguously post-typing; the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup attribution is fuzzier. The qualitative claim ("typing under lossy is a small slice, meta-store bookkeeping dominates") holds either way.

fr:title.text: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Explore a streamlined setup for logical relations: work with a small category \mathcal {GC} whose objects are categories equipped with a groupoid object (or, equivalently, categories in which every map is invertible in the relevant sense), and whose morphisms are the appropriate structure-preserving functors. Define fibrations as functors into \mathcal {GC}. Because each fiber is a groupoid-enriched 1-category, \mathcal {GC} itself is a 1-category — there are no higher coherences to manage.

Motivation. The current displayed-category machinery in Finishing Logical Relations on Display spends a lot of effort on coherences that evaporate once the fibers are forced to be (truncated to) groupoidal. If the target 1-category is rich enough to express the constructions needed for canonicity and normalization logical relations, this may be a lighter foundation than the thickened / displayed-double-category route.

html:ol.html:li: Define the small 1-category \mathcal {GC} of categories-with-groupoid-objects and verify it is a 1-category (no higher cells).
Define fibrations as functors E \to \mathcal {GC} and relate them to the displayed-category presentation already in the library.
Encode the universal properties needed for semantics: terminal / binary products / exponentials at the base, plus their fiberwise analogues.
Encode universal quantification (right adjoint to pullback / reindexing) internally to this framework.
State and prove Beck--Chevalley for the relevant pullback squares.
State and prove Frobenius reciprocity for the left-adjoint / existential direction.
Reconstruct the canonicity logical relation in this framework as a first test case.
Reconstruct the normalization logical relation in this framework as a harder stress test.

html:ul.html:li: What exactly is the right notion of "groupoid object" here — an internal groupoid, a hom-groupoid enrichment, or truncation of hom-sets to sets? The choice affects whether \mathcal {GC} is genuinely small.
Does the 1-categorical structure survive once we add the universal-quantifier / Beck--Chevalley / Frobenius data, or do higher coherences creep back in through the adjoints?
How does this compare to the displayed-category-with-isos setup in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/ and the thickened displayed categories of PR 253?

Given a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over a category \mathcal {C} and a functor F : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C}, the reindexing of \overline {\mathcal {C}} along F is a displayed category over \mathcal {D}. It is simply the portion of \overline {\mathcal {C}} over the image of F.

fr:title.text: Interpretation of a Quiver into a Category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Interpretation of a Quiver into a Category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a Quiver Q and a category C, an interpretation of Q in C, written \iota : Q \rightsquigarrow C, is a graph homomorphism from Q into the underlying graph of C.

Likewise, for a displayed category C^{\mathtt {D}} we can define a displayed interpretation of Q in C^{\mathtt {D}} in a straightforward manner, written \iota ^{\mathtt {D}} : Q \rightsquigarrow C^{\mathtt {D}}.

fr:title.text: Free Monoidal Category over a Set

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Free Monoidal Category over a Set

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix a set X. The objects of the free monoidal category over X, \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}}, are generated inductively by the the elements of X and a unit element I over a binary operation \otimes . The morphisms are given by a quotient-inductive type. They are generated by associators, unitors, and identity over composition and parallel action over \otimes then quotiented by associativity and composition equation to satisfy the category laws, equations constraining the associators/unitors to be natural isomorphisms, and pentagon/triangle equations to satiate the axioms of a Monoidal Category.

fr:title.text: Global Elimination Principle for the Free Monoidal Category

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Global Elimination Principle for the Free Monoidal Category

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given any displayed monoidal category M^{\mathtt {D}} over \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}} with an interpretation \iota : X \rightsquigarrow M^{\mathtt {D}}, we may construct a global section \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}} \to M^{\mathtt {D}}. We refer to this as the global elimination principle of \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}}.

fr:title.text: The Coherence Theorem for Monoidal Categories using Displayed Category Theory

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Coherence Theorem for Monoidal Categories using Displayed Category Theory

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The coherence theorem for monoidal categories can be formulated as saying that the free monoidal category is thin.
We can prove this statement in a few steps. We first invoke the following two lemmas,

fr:title.text: Retraction Lemma for the Coherence Theorem

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Retraction Lemma for the Coherence Theorem

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix a set X. Given a monodial category M, a strong monoidal functor F : M \to \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}}, and an interpretation \iota : X \rightsquigarrow \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}} we can use the global elimination principle of the free monoidal category to construct a global section of \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}}. Then by using the universal property of IsoFiber, we can extract the construction of a functor G : \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}} \to M such that F \circ G \cong \mathsf {Id}.
If D is thin and there are functors F : C \to D and G : D \to C such that G \circ F \cong \mathsf {Id}, then C is also thin.

That is, we reduce the problem to finding a thin monoidal category M with a strong monoidal functor F : M \to \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}}, and an interpretation \iota : X \rightsquigarrow \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}}.

From here, we can construct such a category by using a discrete category of lists over X. This category is discrete (the only morphisms are identities), so it is trivally thin. Further, this category of lists can be shown to have a weak initiality property that gives a strong monoidal functor into any monoidal category interpreting X. In particular, \mathsf {FreeMon}{\mathopen {}\left (X\right )\mathclose {}} interprets X so we get the desired strong monoidal functor F. From here we can also construct such an \iota and complete the proof, but this is somewhat uninspired without going further into details.
The bulk of the proof is really in showing that this category of lists has the weak initiality property, so I should write that up as well.

When conducting metatheoretic proofs on paper, we often appeal to powerful abstractions to succinctly perform a construction. Not only are these abstractions convenient and effective, but for sufficiently complex constructions they are necessary for bookkeeping purposes.

We have known for decades that the appropriate abstractions for this technique are found within category theory. Functorial/fibrational ideas from the study of categorical logic are used to define denotational semantics of programming languages and even notions of program logic over a given language (a la hyperdoctrines). These reusable and abstract principles readily apply on paper, however we have been inable to reap the benefits from this level of abstraction when mechanizing results in a proof assistant.

One roadblock to elegant formalizations of this fibrational ideas is the presence of a propositional equality in the definiton of a Grothendieck fibration. The concept of a displayed category allows for a type-theoretic presentation of a functor/fibration without mentioning the propositional equality in the classical presentation of a Grothendieck fibration. That is, it is a presentation of the same ideas that elides an equality altogether. For this reason, it is preferrable to encode fibrational constructs within type theory (that is, within the proof assistant) within the framework of displayed categories.

For this reason, in Cubical Agda we formalize the displayed-category-theoretic infrastructure necessary to conduct proofs of programming languages metatheory at a level of abstraction comparable to the effective techniques that have been leverage on paper for decades.

We give canonicity and conservativity theorems as instantiations of this common foundation. These proofs demonstrate a reusable formalization strategy for gluing logical relations. Additionally, we give a proof of the coherence theorem for monoidal categories, which can be viewed as a kind of normalization theorem.

Each of these will serve as examples, but I am unsure how best to organize the paper. The introduction ought to motivate the importance of compositional libraries that emulate the structure of elegant paper proofs. It should also mention Review related approaches to metatheory.

The body of the paper should demonstrate the foundational principles of the framework and then later go into precise instantiation with the examples. As future work, we may want different formalisms like (simple) categories with families (which allow for encoding metatheory about not just simple types but also dependent types), richer theorems like normalization or parametricity, and different kinds of languages like substructural languages which require different categorical structures.

The framework then breaks down as follows:
A free category perhaps with some structure, expressed as a category with a (global) dependent elimination principle phrased as the existence of a global section for displayed categories with the displayed variant of the appropriate structure
Often a local elimination principle can arise by showing preservation of displayed structure along reindexing. We need to prove this reindexing theorem for the desired structure. Then the local eliminator is implemented as the global eliminator acting upon the reindexed displayed category
Often we can state the displayed (or global) notion of structure as the one that arises when stating the total category of the displayed category has the oridinary structure. That is, a displayed carteisan category is one whose total category is cartesian. Similarly, we may give a vertical (or local; or fiberwise) notion of the same structure as stating that each fiber category has the appropriate structure. Then provided that the displayed category has enough cartesian lifts (say, is a Grothendieck fibration) we can induce a displayed structure from the vertical one. We may call this a local-to-global principle.
With these components, we may conduct canonicity/conservativity/coherence proofs within the same framework. They each provide their own free category and universal property, then the rest of the proof uses the same infrastructure of displayed categories, reindexing, etc.
Use Gluing for Type Theory as an example for how these things go on paper
